transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-03-07
- Time: 09:32 PT
- Duration: 54 minutes
- Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Derek Cho (Redwood SE), Nina Rao (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (CTO, StrataKern), Ethan Ross (Platform Eng), Li Wei (SRE), Carlos Mendez (Security)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on how StrataKern would route requests through their gateway/proxy, SDK and LangChain/LlamaIndex support, and security/compliance implications for a Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployment. Action items and a 48h perf test were agreed.

Topics:
- SDK language support and drop-in adapters for LangChain and LlamaIndex
- Gateway/proxy architecture and onramp patterns (sidecar vs gateway vs edge proxy)
- Rate limits/quotas and tenant-level enforcement
- Observability hooks, tracing, and token-level cost telemetry
- Security: SSO/SAML, KMS, audit logs, SOC2

Transcript:
[00:00] Ava Martinez: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, quick intros. I'm Ava, AE on the Redwood team.
[00:12] Maya Patel: Hi, Maya here, CTO at StrataKern. We've got Ethan, Li and Carlos with me.
[00:18] Derek Cho: Derek, Redwood SE, I'll jump into the architecture details.
[00:22] Ethan Ross: Morning. We're mostly here because we need clarity on how your SDKs slot into our gateway-based flow. We run an internal API gateway and want minimal changes.
[00:35] Ava Martinez: Yep totally, that's what we hear a lot. We support hosted, dedicated and private, and our SDKs are designed to be used either client-side in microservices or as a server-side adapter behind a gateway. Derek, want to give the quick dev flow?
[00:47] Derek Cho: Sure. At a high level, you can call Redwood's REST API directly from your service using our SDKs for Node/Python/Go, or you can put a small adapter—like a lightweight proxy—next to your gateway that handles batching, retry logic and auth. For LangChain and Lama- sorry, LlamaIndex, we have connector examples that map the chain/agent calls to Redwood endpoints. Note: the connector for LlamaIndex has a couple of name mismatches in older examples, so use the 2026-02 branch.
[01:18] Li Wei: When you say "adapter", is that a sidecar container or a separate microservice? Our infra team prefers sidecar to avoid another hop.
[01:25] Derek Cho: It can be both. We ship a sidecar Helm chart if you want it as sidecar in k8s, but we also provide a stateless gateway proxy image if you prefer centralizing. Sidecars let you do per-pod batching and local KV cache hits; central proxies are easier for rule-based routing and quotas.
[01:44] Maya Patel: Our traffic is bursty—peak 200 qps for short windows, baseline 15 qps. We care about tail latency and also per-tenant cost. How do you enforce quotas?
[01:56] Nina Rao: For Hosted, quotas are enforced at token and request level in our control plane; you can set per-API-key and per-tenant caps. For Dedicated or Private, we provide a policy engine that can be deployed in your VPC which integrates with your identity provider and tenant mapping. You can either push quota rules via API or sync from your existing billing system.
[02:20] Ethan Ross: Do your SDKs expose hooks for our existing rate-limiter so we can short-circuit before calling Redwood to save cost?
[02:29] Derek Cho: Yes, SDK includes pre-call hooks and a cacheable policy decision point. We also recommend prefix-KV caching for repeated prompt contexts—saves tokens. There's also an onramp pattern where your gateway checks local quota, then forwards eligible requests to Redwood adapter which batches them.
[02:50] Li Wei: About batching—our prompts vary 80–120 tokens typically but sometimes go to 1k. Does batching hurt latency for small prompts?
[02:59] Derek Cho: We do continuous batching with adaptive windows. By default, small prompts get sent quickly, batching threshold is microseconds to a few hundred ms depending on throughput; you can tune that in the Helm values. For Dedicated you can pin instance pools to reduce variance.
[03:18] Carlos Mendez: Security question: If we go Dedicated or Private on prem, how do you handle KMS? We need HSM-backed keys and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.
[03:27] Nina Rao: For Private deployments we have KMS integrations—both cloud KMS and HSM via customer key wrap. Audit logs are configurable; we can stream to S3 or syslog and integrate with Splunk/Datadog. We also support envelope encryption so tokens aren't stored in plaintext in the control plane.
[03:45] Maya Patel: Any compliance certifications? SOC2?
[03:48] Ava Martinez: Redwood's hosted control plane is SOC2 Type II. For Private, you control compliance posture but we provide artifacts and assistance during audits. I'll share the security pack.
[03:57] Ethan Ross: On the LangChain/LlamaIndex side—we use LangChain in Python heavily and some LlamaIndex chucks for retrieval. How opinionated are your connectors? Will we need to rewrite our agents?
[04:08] Derek Cho: Minimal changes. Our LangChain adapter implements the standard LLM interface; for LlamaIndex you'll map the retriever to Redwood embeddings and the query pipeline to the text-generation endpoint. Edge case: conversation state and KV cache keys—older LlamaIndex examples use a different conversation id naming convention; we'll share a patch one-off.
[04:30] Ava Martinez: Also, we have plug-and-play embeddings endpoints so you can switch model variants without changing your retriever code.
[04:36] Li Wei: Observability—how granular is your telemetry? We need per-token cost, token breakdown by prompt vs completion, request trace ids, and span info for distributed traces.
[04:48] Nina Rao: We emit trace ids and span correlations which you can forward to your APM. We return token counts per request in the response metadata and also emit structured logs with token cost breakdown. For higher retention we have an add-on.
[05:04] Ethan Ross: Do you provide a Prometheus exporter?
[05:07] Derek Cho: Yep, for Dedicated and Private you can enable a Prometheus exporter with metrics for queue depth, batch sizes, avg token latency, tail percentile latency, and token throughput. Hosted also exposes tenant-level metrics via our dashboard and an ingestion API.
[05:23] Maya Patel: Latency SLOs—our app needs 95th under 300ms for short prompts. Can redwood guarantee that on Hosted?
[05:33] Ava Martinez: Hosted depends on model choice and region—smaller open models hit lower latency. If you need strict SLOs we recommend Dedicated where you reserve capacity and we can provide SLA-backed latency windows. We can model expected p95 in the sizing worksheet.
[05:50] Li Wei: If we do Dedicated with an on-prem runner, what's the upgrade process? We can't have long windows of downtime.
[05:58] Nina Rao: Rolling upgrades are supported, with canary routing and traffic draining. You can control rollout percentages via the console. For Private on-prem we've done zero-downtime upgrades with dual-runway rollout in previous customers.
[06:14] Ethan Ross: Pricing—how is cost modeled when using on-gateway batching vs calling directly?
[06:20] Ava Martinez: Cost is per token for generation/embeddings on Hosted; batching doesn't change token billing but reduces egress and can improve throughput so overall effective cost drops. For Dedicated you pay reserved capacity plus a unit token rate; we can show example math in the worksheet.
[06:36] Maya Patel: Are there cordon-off controls for sensitive data? Some of our prompts include PII and PHI. We need guaranteed no-user-data-retention for some tenants.
[06:46] Nina Rao: We support per-tenant retention policies and redaction hooks at the adapter layer. In Private you can configure zero retention. For Hosted we have retention lock settings and DLP integration as an add-on.
[07:00] Ethan Ross: Quick technical: does your runtime support kv cache snapshotting when pods evict? We sometimes see jitter and don't want to lose long conversation contexts.
[07:09] Derek Cho: We persist KV cache on a local fast store and optionally sync to a shared cache like Redis. The sidecar supports a safe flush policy; on Dedicated we can recommend using local NVMe-backed cache with Redis fallback. We'll share a sample helm value for the cache policy.
[07:28] Li Wei: Any gotchas with GRPC vs HTTP? Our gateway does gRPC+envoy.
[07:33] Derek Cho: We support both; gRPC gives you streaming and lower overhead. Our SDK exposes a gRPC client for Node and Go—Python uses a gRPC stub too. Note: if you route via Envoy you'll want to disable HTTP/2 multiplexing for streaming to keep spans aligned. We'll provide recommended Envoy filters.
[07:53] Maya Patel: For the PoC we want to validate three things: integration effort, p95 latency on our traffic profile, and cost per 1M tokens. Can you run a perf smoke test?
[08:03] Derek Cho: Yes. We'll run a 48-hour medium-load test using your sample prompts. We'll deploy the sidecar model into a staging namespace and hit it through your gateway if you can provide a kubeconfig or an ephemeral tunnel.
[08:16] Ethan Ross: We can stand up a staging cluster and give you access. We prefer not to share full prod kconfig.
[08:22] Ava Martinez: That's fine. For security questionnaire we'll need the usual contacts—Carlos, you'll be our security point?
[08:27] Carlos Mendez: Yep. I'll get the questionnaire back within a week, but I need more detail on audit log formats.
[08:33] Nina Rao: We'll attach sample log schemas and a Splunk ingestion example.
[08:38] Li Wei: One more—how do you handle model fallbacks? If our preferred model is down or overloaded, can requests failover to a cheaper model without dev changes?
[08:49] Derek Cho: Yes, smart routing policies. You can define fallback chains at the project level—automatic fallback to a compatible quantized variant, different region, or lower-cost family. You can also set quality thresholds and Canary policies to ensure regressions are limited.
[09:04] Maya Patel: Great. Any limitations with LlamaIndex in terms of retrieval-augmented generation?
[09:09] Derek Cho: The main thing is chunk size and embedding model. Make sure you pick an embeddings model whose tokenization aligns with your retriever chunking—otherwise semantic drift appears. We recommend a short test comparing cosine similarity on your dataset.
[09:26] Ethan Ross: Regarding quotas enforcement again—do you support burst buffers? We have sudden spikes for ingestion pipelines.
[09:33] Nina Rao: There's a burst allowance in Dedicated, configurable by pool. Hosted has burst buckets too but limited by VM capacity. For strict production patterns, Dedicated with reserved extra headroom is the pattern we recommend.
[09:48] Ava Martinez: Ok, to recap next steps: Derek & team will prepare the perf script and example helm values; I'll send the security pack and pricing worksheet; Maya/Carlos will return the security questionnaire and staging kubeconfig.
[10:00] Maya Patel: Sounds good. One ask: can you include a short sample of the LangChain adapter with our multi-step agent? We do some tool-calling.
[10:08] Derek Cho: Absolutely — we'll provide an agent example with function/tool-calling mapped to your internal tool endpoints and a LangChain callback for tracing.
[10:17] Ethan Ross: If everything looks good after perf, we're aiming to start a 3-month pilot and then decide on Dedicated vs Private based on results.
[10:25] Ava Martinez: Perfect. We'll aim to have the materials in 48 hours and the perf run scheduled within a week.
[10:33] Meeting ended.
